title: CASE OF RENOLDE v. FRANCE
conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (non-exhaustion of domestic remedies);Violation of Art. 2 (procedural aspect);Violation of Art. 3 (substantive aspect)
summary: In the case of Renolde v. France, the applicant, Ms. Renolde, is the sister of Joselito Renolde, both members of a Traveller family, who brought a case against France following her brother’s death in custody. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals in detention, especially those with mental health issues, and the risks they face when their specific needs are not adequately addressed by authorities. Joselito Renolde, who had a history of psychiatric problems, was placed in pre-trial detention in April 2000 and later transferred to Bois-d’Arcy Prison. Despite a suicide attempt and clear signs of acute mental distress, he was placed in a punishment cell for 45 days after a disciplinary incident, with insufficient supervision of his medication and mental health. On 20 July 2000, Joselito Renolde died by suicide in his cell. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 2 (right to life) and Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found France in violation of both articles, citing failures in the authorities’ duty to protect Joselito’s life and to ensure humane treatment. This judgment is significant as it underscores the heightened duty of care owed to vulnerable detainees, particularly from Roma and Traveller backgrounds, in a context where such minorities have historically faced neglect and discrimination in European custodial settings.
